Walk

Adampol: a Polish Village by the Bosphorus

9 stops · about 2 h · on foot

Adampol, today Polonezköy: a village founded in 1842 on the initiative of Prince Adam Jerzy Czartoryski in the forests of the Asian shore. The walk runs from the village centre and the memorial to Atatürk's visit, past the Zofia Ryży memory house, to the Church of Our Lady of Częstochowa with the founders' and Mickiewicz plaques, then on to the Polish cemetery and the forest of the nature park.

Stops

  1. Adampol (Polonezköy) village centre

    Beykoz · 1842–

    A Polish village above the Bosphorus, founded in 1842 at Prince Adam Czartoryski's wish for countrymen without a country – and still alive more than 180 years on.

  2. Memorial of Atatürk's 1937 visit

    Beykoz · 1937

    Village musicians played a krakowiak for Atatürk – and legend has it that the President then joined the dance.

  3. Zofia Ryży Memorial House ('Aunt Zosia's House')

    Beykoz · 1881–1883 / 1940

    To the whole village she was 'Aunt Zosia' – and, Poland's ambassador said, it was thanks to her that Polish did not die out in Adampol.

  4. Founders' memorial, 150th anniversary (Czartoryski and Czajkowski)

    Beykoz · 1842 / 1992

    'A Polish village on Turkish soil' – so says the stone that 'grateful Adampol residents and compatriots from Poland' raised to the village's founders on its 150th anniversary.

  5. Adam Mickiewicz memorial plaque (1933)

    Beykoz · 1933

    'To our Bard' – in 1933 a Polish village near Istanbul honoured Mickiewicz with a plaque in two languages, calling him in Turkish 'our great poet'.

  6. Church of Our Lady of Częstochowa

    Beykoz · 1846 / 1914

    The church this Polish village waited almost twenty years for, built in 1914 with money collected in Poland – where in 1941 the future Pope John XXIII confirmed the village children.

  7. Polish Catholic Cemetery, Polonezköy

    Beykoz · 1853–

    A cemetery the settlers cleared with their own hands – the resting place of insurgents, Crimean War veterans and generations of villagers.

  8. Grave of Ludwika Śniadecka

    Beykoz · 1866

    The young Słowacki's first love and Sadyk Pasha's companion rests at Adampol – 'on Polish soil', as her epitaph says.

  9. Polonezköy Nature Park

    Beykoz · 1842 / 1994

    Walk the same forest the first settlers of Adampol entered more than 180 years ago – today some 3,000 protected hectares of oak, chestnut and beech.
